decisions.quote: The note- and test-taking skills of typically functioning undergraduates are significantly and positively related to handwriting speed, listening comprehension, background knowledge and sustained attention. This study attempted to replicate these findings with two groups of high school students—those with and without the diagnosis of a learning disability (LD).
decisions.reason: The supplied primary source text (093f9256cef7606a.txt) consists only of the title, authors, and abstract, and no prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In the abstract, Oefinger and Peverly state: 'The note- and test-taking skills of typically functioning undergraduates are significantly and positively related to handwriting speed, listening comprehension, background knowledge and sustained attention. This study attempted to replicate these findings with two groups of high school students—those with and without the diagnosis of a learning disability (LD).' However, the abstract does not cite any specific author, year, title, or DOI. Shipped row input_row_index 132 is Peverly, Vekaria, Reddington, Sumowski, Johnson, and Ramsay (2012), 'The Relationship of Handwriting Speed, Working Memory, Language Comprehension and Outlines to Lecture Note‐taking and Test‐taking among College Students' (10.1002/acp.2881, verified in bibliography_metadata.json). Because Peverly and colleagues published multiple studies on undergraduate lecture note-taking and the predictors listed in the abstract (handwriting speed, listening comprehension, background knowledge, and sustained attention) do not identical-match the predictors named in the title of shipped row 132 (handwriting speed, working memory, language comprehension, and outlines), the precise unresolved question is whether the unnamed undergraduate study (or studies) replicated here is shipped row input_row_index 132, another Peverly et al. paper, or multiple papers, which cannot be settled from the abstract alone without the full text and reference list.
